business_problem: EDF's internally built Customer Analytics Zone made secure access to sensitive data and production deployment of machine-learning models too slow, forcing data scientists to wait on extracts and stretching customer-intelligence projects from weeks into months.
solution_summary: EDF replaced its bespoke Customer Analytics Zone with the Intelligent Customer Engine on Snowflake to make sensitive customer data available for governed analytics and machine learning. Customer and operational data now lands in Snowflake as a central repository, where data scientists use Snowpark for Python to do feature engineering directly where the data sits instead of waiting on lake-team extracts. Models are then pushed into production on Amazon SageMaker through EDF's AWS setup, giving the company a repeatable path for customer-intelligence workloads. The platform supports use cases such as identifying financially vulnerable customers, targeting the right products and prices, and exposing smart-meter insights through customer-facing energy hub analytics. Because storage and compute scale independently, EDF can keep secure enterprise data accessible, build products in weeks instead of months, and evolve ICE as a shared analytics environment rather than as a one-off ML platform.

data_flow: Customer and operational data is centralized in Snowflake, where data scientists use Snowpark for Python for feature engineering and model preparation. Amazon SageMaker then runs production ML models that feed EDF's Intelligent Customer Engine, financially vulnerable customer identification workflows, and customer-facing energy-usage analytics.
business_outcome: EDF built its Intelligent Customer Engine in two months, accelerated new product delivery from months to three or four weeks, projected up to four times more data products per year, and improved how it supports vulnerable customers and energy-efficiency experiences.
